statement: This is the 16th cohort of the course: eight weeks of system design aimed at building raw intuition for systems, always focusing on the implementation side rather than just drawing boxes.
detail: The teacher does not believe in drawing boxes: going into the intricate details of a system is what makes engineers better; boxes 'you can do as a kid also'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll always talk about the implementation side of things rather than just drawing boxes. I don't believe in drawing boxes.

statement: Participate live in every session, no matter what: live sessions involve active brainstorming, which rewires the brain to think about systems intuitively rather than in question-and-answer form.
detail: Even with commitments, take out time to attend live; the discipline is what gets the most out of the course. The teacher took sessions despite very unfortunate incidents. It is called the first and most important point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: participate live no matter what happens.

statement: The course does not talk about interviews (the teacher does not believe anyone should prepare for interviews); its goals are the joy of engineering and the intuition to build any system in the world, using first principles and simple designs that scale the way real-world systems are built.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I want everyone to feel the joy of engineering, number one. Number two, build intuition to build any system in the world.

statement: Note down new terms heard in class (e.g. sharding, consistent hashing) and read about them later on your own; this is an intermediate course, so the teacher explains many things but expects self-study of unknown ones.
detail: The teacher avoids jargon and keeps things simple, but some things have names that cannot be simplified.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you'll hear a lot of new terms, and it's very much possible that you would not have heard it in the past

statement: Revise regularly: the course is chained week to week, so by week 7 (ad hoc systems such as flash sale and message brokers) the earlier weeks' learnings make those systems simple - a flash sale takes about 10 minutes max to design.
detail: In most cases there is a string connecting all the systems; take out time to revise if needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: flash sale 10 minutes max will take to design it. It's that simple.

statement: Read the pre-reads: they are heavily curated for each session's topics and give most of what is needed to follow the session.
detail: The teacher calls it extremely important; 'two months is nothing, just give it all'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then read the pre-reads. Extremely important, because the pre-reads are very heavily curated for the session that we would have.

statement: Each participant has three one-on-ones with the teacher, bookable from the 'discuss one-on-one' section beneath the video on the course platform.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have three one-on-ones to leverage.

statement: System design is not just drawing boxes and does not need massive infrastructure: literally every system discussed in the course is implementable on a local machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every single system that we discuss is implementable on a local machine. You don't need fancy infrastructure to do it.

statement: Implement the core of every system discussed (e.g. the flash-sale module itself, not the UI or every CRUD API), taking a year or a year and a half; people who have done it see huge results.
detail: Not expected during the course itself; take your time and absorb everything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Implement the core of the system, for example, flash sale, right?

statement: Implementing a system reveals where it could falter and what implementation challenges arise ('the devil lies in the details'), and in real-world organizations engineers are expected to implement, not just draw boxes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you don't need to implement the entire system, but implement a core of it, because the devil lies in the details.

statement: After every session the teacher shares a Google form with two questions - what worked for you, and what can be done better - and uses it to tune the delivery for each cohort.
detail: Every cohort is unique and the pace is adjusted to the people in it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: after every session, I share one link to Google form having two questions.

statement: The Discord server has a channel called 'Look What I Found' where participants share interesting articles, videos and resources; the first link ever shared there was AOSN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is a Discord channel called Look What I Found. Share it there.

statement: Sessions run Saturday and Sunday, 9 to 11:30 a.m.; the core content is covered by about 11:30, then an open forum continues until every doubt is answered (one session went until 1:30).
detail: Brainstorming also happens in the middle of sessions. Accept the calendar invite to get notifications.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: sessions would not end until I have answered all the doubts

statement: Recordings are available on the learning portal learn.relog.in by the end of the day (11:59 p.m.), because they take time to transcode and to fix audio glitches.
detail: Also join the Discord server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You go to that and access all the recordings. The recordings will be shared by the end of the day.

statement: Each session is split into sections, with questions taken at the end of each section as time permits; any remaining doubts go to the open forum after 11:30.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each session has a bunch of sections, and at the end of each section, I'll, we take questions.

statement: There is no system brainstorming in the first week, so that everyone reaches the same level on the foundations; brainstorming of systems starts from the second week, with Q&A throughout.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First week, I don't do any because I want everyone to be on the same level.

statement: The teacher's YouTube videos (real-world system design and architectures) and a new membership are recommended extras, but nothing covered in the course is published there; the course is the teacher's top content.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But be assured, nothing that I cover in my course will be out there.

statement: Other resources: a separate course on Redis internals, and essays from 2020, when the teacher read one research paper every week, wrote about it in depth and mostly implemented it (e.g. pseudo random number generators, terrain generation algorithms).
detail: The essays are on the teacher's website (top right, 'essays'), separate from the newsletter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Entire 2020 I read one research paper every week and I wrote about it in depth

statement: Today's agenda has two parts: first, designing an online/offline indicator (as on Facebook or Twitter); after the break, how to approach system design, covering databases and caching in the context of building a Medium-like application.
detail: The second half uses very simple concepts but goes into the granular details every engineer should know.
case_study: The second half (databases, caching) is set in a Medium-like blogging application.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll start with designing the online offline indicator.

statement: On day one the online/offline indicator is designed without worrying about scale (the design would change once later concepts are covered); performance improvements are still discussed, and scale comes in weeks two to four.
detail: Even if the solution feels obvious, the point is the implementation specifics and forming the core intuition for building any system, from first principles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll still talk about performance improvements, but not scale because you need, we'll go in the second, third, fourth week.

statement: The brief from the product team: show a list of users, each with a green dot (online) or a grey dot (offline), as Facebook and Twitter do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Green dots implies they are online. Grey dots implies they are offline.

statement: In 10-11 years the teacher has seen only two approaches to building any system - spiral and incremental; which one to use depends on the system, and there is no hard rule.
detail: The course uses both: spiral in some places, incremental in others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've only seen two ways, two categories of approaches, or rather two approaches in general to build any system.

statement: Spiral approach: decide the core of the system - in most cases the database - which becomes its single point of focus, then build components around it as needed (database, then API servers, then a load balancer, and so on).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you decide the core of your system, which becomes the single point of focus of your system

statement: The core of a system can be a database schema or a communication layer; in a messaging app the WebSocket layer is the core and everything is built around it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Messaging app, then your WebSocket becomes the core of the system and then you build everything around it.

statement: Incremental approach: used when unsure how to implement or scale; start with the simplest day-zero architecture (e.g. user, load balancer, API server, database), see how each component behaves under load and at scale, identify the borderline, re-architect, and repeat until content.
detail: Decisions along the way include whether a server is overburdened and whether to split it into another service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you start with the day zero architecture, whatever simplistic thing ever.

statement: Use the spiral approach when the system is a no-brainer - you have built similar systems before and know exactly how things will transpire.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you have built similar systems before, you typically go with spiral because you exactly know how things would transpire.

statement: Use the incremental approach in ambiguous or uncertain situations; it resonates with startup environments: ship a day-zero architecture to some users and re-architect over time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can typically see how incremental building resonates with startup like environment.

statement: In a multi-year project at a big organization, where you know what you need to implement and it is complex, you typically start with some parts and grow organically around them; there are no hard lines between the approaches - knowing both gives confidence when building.
detail: Which approach 'this' refers to is not explicit in the audio.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In a multi-year project at a big organization you typically go with this, where you know what you need to implement
flags: check: which approach 'this' refers to for multi-year projects at big organizations (board?)

statement: For every technical decision, first understand the core property and access pattern you need from the component, then see which tools fit; do not choose by affinity ('I'll use Redis because I love Redis', or only Postgres, DynamoDB or Cassandra) - that rigidity hampers the system's growth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: first, understand the core property and access pattern. Really important.

statement: Tech affinity fails in practice: a company not on AWS cannot use DynamoDB, and a company that does not use Redis still needs the system built - so pick whatever satisfies the requirement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whatever company is not on AWS, you cannot use DynamoDB, right?

statement: Throughout the course the teacher discards Cassandra in many places: for simple use cases a relational DB can solve it, and, counterintuitively, there are systems operating at scale built on relational DBs instead of Cassandra.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I literally discard Cassandra. We don't need that kind of fancy stuff.

statement: Build intuition for building systems: there is no single way to build a system - every system is infinitely buildable and can evolve - and in the real world you will have to build systems that do not exist yet, which is where intuition matters most.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every system is infinitely buildable. You can evolve it the way you want.

statement: The online/offline indicator design starts by picking the database as the core of the system (spiral approach), the easiest place to start, asking what is needed to render a user with a green or grey indicator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say we pick our core of the system as database. That's the easiest one to start.

statement: First schema: for every user store the user ID (an integer) and an online boolean (true = online, false = offline).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'll store it as an integer because user ID integer, fair assumption, and online or offline. So I'll store a boolean, true or false.

statement: The access pattern is key-value: get the status of a set of users, get the status of a single user, update the status of a single user - this identifies the access pattern, not yet the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is a classic key-value use case. It's just access pattern. It's not kind of database.

statement: An API server queries the database; the first option is an endpoint that takes one user ID and returns that user's status.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First is given a user, give me the status.

statement: With only a single-user endpoint, rendering four users on the UI needs four API calls from the front end - a very poor experience, and the large number of API calls burdens the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you will have to make four API calls from the front end. Very poor experience

statement: First critical design decision: expose a batch endpoint that accepts a bunch of user IDs and returns the status of all of them, reducing the front end's network calls while the backend does the heavy lifting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the first critical design decision that we'll take is we'll expose a batch endpoint.

statement: The batch endpoint is /data/users, accepting a set of IDs and returning the online/offline status of each; this settles the rendering side.
detail: Understanding why an endpoint is exposed a certain way is one of the 'intricate details' the course cares about, rather than just drawing boxes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we expose the endpoint slash data slash users and we accept a bunch of IDs there.

statement: Reading is solved; someone must also update each user's online/offline information, and there are two ways to get it: pull or push.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now someone has to update this information because reading is done. What about updating?

statement: A pull-based model, where the API server asks each client 'are you alive?', is not possible: HTTP is stateless with no persistent connection, so the API server cannot talk to the client - the client has to talk to the server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But that is not possible because HTTP stateless, there is no persistent connection, so API server cannot talk to client.

statement: Push-based heartbeats: each client periodically makes a heartbeat API call telling the backend 'I am alive'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So periodically you would send heartbeats to the backend and say that I am alive.

statement: A heartbeat mimics the human heart: as long as the heart is beating you are alive; when it stops, you are dead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So long as the heart is beating, you are alive. Heart stops beating, you are dead, right?

statement: Expose a POST /heartbeat endpoint; each call marks the authenticated user as alive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You expose the endpoint slash heartbeat on which you can pass in post and say that whatever the authenticated user is will be...

statement: A common idea is that two calls suffice - one heartbeat when the user comes online / logs in and one 'offline' call at logout - instead of periodic heartbeats.
detail: Rejected in the next item: a client cannot reliably report going offline.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if I send it once when I'm online and once when I log out?

statement: Heartbeats must be periodic because a client can announce coming online but cannot reliably announce going offline: if the machine crashes, the battery dies or the device is unplugged, no offline call is made and the UI keeps showing the user online.
detail: This is described as a very common case and a fundamental limitation: you are not in control of making an API call just before the device dies.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can tell when you are online, but offline you cannot tell because you are not in that control

statement: If the backend does not receive a heartbeat from a user for long enough, it marks the user offline - the most natural progression of the design.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if the backend does not receive a heartbeat for a long enough time, then the backend would say that this user is offline.

statement: 'Long enough' is business logic configured per system - e.g. 10 minutes for one system, 10 seconds or one minute for others; this design uses 30 seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For some system it would be in 10 minutes, if I don't receive a heartbeat, I'll mark this user as offline.

statement: The schema changes: instead of a boolean, store the time the last heartbeat was received for each user (table 'pulse': user ID, last heartbeat), updated on every POST /heartbeat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So instead of storing bool what we store is we store the time at which we received the last heartbeat.

statement: Convention: a table drawn on the board only helps visualize the schema and does not mean a relational database; SQL written in class is just an easy way to explain and does not mean only SQL is used.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever I draw something like this does not mean it is relational.

statement: On each heartbeat run: UPDATE pulse SET last_heartbeat = now() WHERE user_id = <id>, continually updating that user's row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So update pulse set last heartbeat equal to now where user id is equal to something, right?

statement: getStatus logic, rule 1: if there is no entry in the database for a user, return offline - the user never came online.
detail: The getStatus business logic becomes a bit more complex once the last-heartbeat time is stored instead of a boolean; the same logic applies to batch requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if there is no entry in the database for a user, we say it's offline.

statement: getStatus logic, rule 2: if the entry exists but last_heartbeat < now - 30 seconds (no heartbeat for over 30 seconds), return offline; otherwise the user is online.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If there is an entry and entry.lastheartbeat less than now minus 30 seconds

statement: The last heartbeat is stored as epoch seconds - the seconds elapsed since 1 January 1970, the standard Unix epoch.
detail: Introduced while doing a back-of-the-envelope estimate of the system ('seventh standard' mathematics).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This the seconds elapsed from 1st January 1970, which is a standard Unix epoch that we would store over here.

statement: Each row is two integers - user ID and last heartbeat timestamp - 4 bytes + 4 bytes = 8 bytes per user, with one entry per user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 4 byte plus 4 byte is equal to 8 byte.

statement: For 1 billion users (about 1/8 of the world population; Facebook has much more), one 8-byte entry per user gives 8 GB in total.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The total size of this would be one billion entries. Each entry is eight bytes. So the total size is eight GB.

statement: 8 GB is not much - a phone has 128 GB and it fits in the RAM of a trivial, cheap machine - so storage is not the challenge for this system; it requires something else.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This system requires something else. Storage is not a challenge for the system.

statement: At every step of designing a system, ask critical questions - can I change this, is there an alternative? - because every system is about analyzing hundreds and thousands of trade-offs and picking the best path.
detail: Raised while hypothetically asking whether the 8 GB could be made smaller even though it is not needed for every system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single system is all about analyzing hundreds and thousands of trade-offs and then picking the best path for yourself.

statement: Stay open to every possibility without bias and be humble: document every possibility you know and why you took a certain path; answering 'no' to 'did you think of this?' earns no brownie points. This is the heart and soul of being a better senior engineer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Be humble, always document every single possibility that you know, and tell why you took a certain path.

statement: Storage optimization: since the end user only sees green or grey dots, treat absence of an entry as offline - an entry exists only for online users - which reduces the rows by a significant margin.
detail: Done even though storage is not a problem, as a hypothetical optimization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So absence of entry in the database is equal to offline.

statement: With absence = offline, entries must expire after 30 seconds: each heartbeat resets the 30-second timer and once it runs out the entry is deleted, so the number of entries equals the number of users online at that moment.
detail: At 00:40:01 the transcript reads 'what if absence is equal to online', apparently a slip, since the logic described is absence = offline.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever I receive a heartbeat, I reset the timer of 30 seconds and then once 30 seconds exhaust, I'll delete those entries.
flags: check: 'absence is equal to online' at 00:40:01 vs 'absence is equal to offline' at 00:38:47

statement: The simplest way to delete expired entries is a cron job that periodically finds rows whose last heartbeat is older than 30 seconds and deletes them; getStatus then just checks whether the entry exists.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's just write a cron job that deletes the expired entries.

statement: The cron-job solution would work for a startup just launching, but it is not robust - edge cases need handling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Would work for a startup when you are just launching out. But it's not a robust solution.

statement: A cron job adds another moving part: a separate process to host that must keep running (or the business logic falters), with its own uptime, monitoring and telemetry to manage alongside the REST service.
detail: The teacher calls this counterintuitive relative to YouTube videos and the internet, where people add random services here and there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you are adding one more moving part in your system. Don't.

statement: Never draw boxes for the sake of it: think from the implementation - would you really want to implement, monitor and manage this component? If not, look for a better alternative. Making a diagram look complex is the worst thing you can do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Making your diagram look complex is the worst thing that you can do.

statement: Instead of a cron job, offload expiration to the database: when databases exist that do this natively, don't reinvent the wheel or add unnecessary components.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: can you offload this to the database? Can your database do this deletion for it?

statement: The requirement is a database with key-value access plus expiration (time to live, TTL); two very common ones are Redis and DynamoDB, chosen specifically (among others) to drive a further discussion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Two very common databases are Redis and DynamoDB.

statement: Final logic: on every heartbeat, upsert the user's entry in Redis or DynamoDB with a TTL of 30 seconds (resetting the TTL); the database deletes it automatically on expiry; entry exists = online, absent = offline. The app is just REST endpoints talking to this database.
detail: This keeps the design extremely simple: the database takes care of the deletion complexity and the team manages the least.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we update the entry in Redis and DynamoDB, whichever DB you choose, with a TTL of 30 seconds.

statement: Redis and DynamoDB both give key-value access and expiration, so choosing between them for this system needs other criteria (the pre-reads asked students to read about both).
detail: Posed to the class as a brainstorming question.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one is Redis, one is, both gives us key-value, both gives us expiration, right?

statement: A student proposed DynamoDB because data might need to be stored permanently (persistence); the teacher challenged it: this data is deleted after 30 seconds anyway, so why would persistence be needed?
detail: The teacher later summarised the student's pick as 'persistence and managed' and said 'That's right'; no explicit verdict on persistence itself.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Why would you need persistence for this? We said that 30 seconds gone, your data is anyway deleted.
flags: check: verdict on the persistence argument (challenged at 00:46:53, 'That's right' at 00:47:58)

statement: A student proposed DynamoDB because it is managed by AWS (highly available), whereas self-managed in-memory Redis can go down; the teacher endorsed it: a managed service offloads infrastructure management to the cloud vendor so the team can focus on business logic.
detail: The student added that with enough money to manage infrastructure, Redis is also an option.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you are offloading the management part to the cloud vendor that you have so that you focus more on the business logic.

statement: A student proposed that choosing a managed solution depends on team size, and that Redis can help prevent vendor lock-in, since DynamoDB locks you into AWS and is harder to migrate off.
detail: The teacher took the vendor lock-in point up and expanded on it.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Redis can help you prevent vendor lock-in if that is a concern that you have
flags: check: fragment, words may be missing

statement: A student listed reasons vendor lock-in can matter - cloud pricing becoming unmanageable, the rest of the infrastructure moving to another provider, better deals elsewhere - while noting it often does not end up being a big issue.
detail: Answering the teacher's 'why is vendor lock-in such a big issue / why would you switch a cloud provider?'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: vendor lock-in can be an issue in case the pricing starts being unmanageable

statement: A student added non-cost reasons to switch cloud providers: security incidents (e.g. issues with Azure databases' access), a bigger concern for banks; and GCP being somewhat infamous for discontinuing services, prompting a move to AWS. The teacher called these valid: vendor mess-ups or loss of trust.
detail: The teacher's summary also mentions finding the vendor too complex to use.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: GCP is a little bit infamous for discontinuing services

statement: Vendor lock-in: being locked in with a particular cloud vendor because the tool you use exists only there - DynamoDB is only on AWS, not GCP or Azure - so moving elsewhere means rewriting your code for another technology.
detail: DynamoDB was picked for this discussion specifically to raise vendor lock-in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: With vendor lock-in, what happens is you cannot move out of that easily because the tool that you are using is only with that.

statement: Moving clouds (GCP to AWS, AWS to Azure, ...) means rewriting a lot of code, which is why organizations that reach a certain maturity think about vendor lock-in a lot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when organizations reach a certain maturity level, they think about vendor locking a lot, right?

statement: A key vendor lock-in reason is competition: if your cloud vendor enters your business, your cloud bill feeds your competitor. E.g. Amazon launched Amazon Foods in India; if Swiggy and Zomato are on AWS (the teacher is not sure), their bills fund Amazon's food business.
detail: This is not fixed in advance: you may already be on AWS when Amazon enters your business.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then they are literally feeding their competitor
flags: teacher hedge: 'I'm not sure what they are on'

statement: Walmart is not on AWS but on GCP, because Walmart and Amazon are both e-commerce competitors - being on AWS would feed its competitor.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is one of the main reasons why for Walmart is not on AWS. They are competitors. Walmart is on GCP, right?

statement: For a big customer with, say, a $10 million/month cloud bill, a vendor entering your business means paying your competitor $10 million a month; Amazon is just one example - Azure/Microsoft, Google and Alibaba are known for this too.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are literally paying your competitor $10 million a month.

statement: A very early startup need not worry about this: with a bill of about $10,000 it does not matter to Amazon; big customers always think about it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you don't have to do it when you're working at a very early start-up, because your bill is ten thousand dollars

statement: Counter-example: Netflix existed before Amazon Prime Video became its competitor, yet it stays on AWS because moving would require rewriting so much code; there is likely a mutual agreement / better deal since Netflix is AWS's biggest customer (the teacher does not know the details).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But one counter example of that, Netflix.
flags: teacher hedge: 'I don't know the details'

statement: Vendor lock-in is a critical real-world design consideration, and is why many people go towards open-source technologies rather than proprietary ones.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is why you see a lot of people going in the open source technologies direction rather than going for something proprietary

statement: A student pointed out that Redis also offers persistence; the teacher agreed it can be configured if needed, with a few limitations.
detail: Another student asked how it is configured; the student cited a blog post shared in chat.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Persistence, Redis gives you persistence. I totally agree on that.

statement: Know how a feature is implemented, not just that it exists: e.g. for Redis persistence know AOF and RDB files, how to configure it and the flush frequency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's good to know that Redis gives you persistence, how they give it, you should know

statement: A student noted that managed Redis is offered by the cloud providers (e.g. AWS ElastiCache), so you get a managed service and can still move between providers because the underlying code stays the same.
detail: 'Okay. Correct.' appears inside the student's own turn, so there is no clear teacher verdict.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you can also move on from one cloud provider to other providers if it is needed, because like the underlying code will be the same.
flags: check: speaker of 'Okay. Correct.' inside student turn at 00:56:36

statement: A student claimed Redis only has string data types while DynamoDB also has numbers.
detail: Correction by the teacher: 'Even Redis has numbers' - Redis is not just strings, it has a bunch of data structures.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Redis only has string data types in, in the terms we are storing.

statement: Consider future extensibility: if the feature may later need advanced data structures - Bloom filters, HyperLogLogs, geospatial queries - you may lean towards Redis, though this may not matter for online/offline.
detail: Reframes the student's data-type point; the teacher calls future extensibility a very good point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: advanced data structures like Bloom filters, like HyperLogLogs, like a geospatial queries and whatnot, which is where Redis comes into play.

statement: A student said DynamoDB can achieve similar things with DynamoDB Streams and Lambda; the teacher agreed, noting databases keep evolving with many features and Redis also offers CDC.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: And when you talk about DynamoDB streams, Redis also gives you CDCs out of that.

statement: Databases are converging fast - every database gives you everything: MongoDB supports ACID, SQL databases support sharding now.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: World is converging really fast. MongoDB supports ACID, SQL support sharding now, everything's happening.

statement: Before deciding, go in depth into every candidate technology, understand its pros and cons, and pick what suits you best; stay open to everything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: before you make decisions, go in depth of every single candidates that you have and understand the pros and cons

statement: A student proposed Redis because online/offline is time-sensitive and Redis, being in-memory with better performance, is faster than DynamoDB (e.g. querying 500 million active users).
detail: Correction by the teacher: 'Not really' - being in memory is not the main reason; the time-sensitivity advantage comes from the persistent connections Redis allows (next item).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Yeah. But why would it be faster? Is it only because it's in memory?

statement: Redis's advantage for time-sensitive use is persistent connections: with Redis you hold persistent connections, giving extremely low latency (at a cost), whereas DynamoDB is stateless and you cannot create persistent connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: With Redis, you create persistent connections, which is what would give you that extreme low latency that you require.

statement: Each database has its own feature set - Redis has Pub/Sub, DynamoDB has its own features, Aerospike (proprietary) has its own - so be open and dive deep into each.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Aerospike is there. Aerospike is proprietary. It has its own bunch of features, right?

statement: The database is the most critical, most brittle component of your infrastructure: know early what features it offers and its performance numbers, and build intuition for using it over time.

statement: To show a user offline immediately when their key expires, Redis gives hooks telling you a key just expired, on the fly over a persistent connection; DynamoDB does not - it exposes expiry through streams, which takes a long time to process.

statement: Redis and DynamoDB were chosen because Redis is open source and DynamoDB proprietary - a big difference; a big organization thinking about vendor lock-in may choose one over the other.

statement: Lean teams (a 5-10 person startup) go for managed services to avoid the pressure of managing infrastructure, or because they lack the expertise: managing any database (MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch) has its own pain points - observability, profiling and more.

statement: Beyond the common answers, three factors are often missed when choosing a database: future extensions, vendor lock-in and managed vs self-managed.
